contrasts.value: what did not happen or has not happened; 有

profile.feeling: Matter-of-fact: something is missing or did not happen.

senses.def: not (before 有; and before a verb: did not, has not)
(short for 没有) not have; there isn’t

examples.tr: He isn't as tall as you.

synonyms.nuance: negates habits, wishes, the future, adjectives and 是
wú: ‘without, there is no’ in written style (无人 ‘nobody’)
wèi: ‘not yet’ in written style (未成年 ‘under age’)

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 水 (‘water’) + phonetic; the character’s old meaning is ‘to sink’. The negator méi is possibly a colloquial variant of 勿 or 未 influenced by 有 — not derived from ‘to sink’ (Schuessler).

funFacts: The traditional form 沒 has 𠬛 on the right; the simplified 没 writes 殳 (几 over 又) instead.
pitfalls: Never *没是 — the negation of 是 is 不是.
Don’t add 了 after 没 + verb: 我没吃 (not *我没吃了).
In 沉没 (chénmò, ‘to sink’) the same character is read mò.
subtleties: 没 describes facts, 不 describes will and habits: 我不吃肉 ‘I don’t eat meat’ vs 我没吃肉 ‘I didn’t eat (the) meat’.

toneSandhi.none: no 一 or 不 in the word

profile.feeling: With a negation: an empty fridge, a child who refuses to eat — nothing at all.

senses.def: (with 不 / 没) nothing, not anything
(without a negation) everything, anything at all

examples.py: Wǒ shénme dōu bù xiǎng chī.
examples.tr: I don’t feel like eating anything.

collocations.tr: there is nothing; to have nothing

synonyms.nuance: shénme yě: the same in negative sentences (什么也没有); 什么都 also works without a negation
méi shénme: ‘nothing much, it’s nothing’ — also a reply to thanks or an apology
yīwúsuǒyǒu: an idiom, ‘to own nothing at all’

etymology.text: 什么 ‘what’ + 都 ‘all’: ‘whatever — all of it’; with a negation, ‘nothing’.

funFacts: Chinese builds ‘nothing, nobody, nowhere’ from question words: 什么都不 ‘nothing’, 谁都不 ‘nobody’, 哪儿都不 ‘nowhere’ — like Russian ничего, никто, нигде from что, кто, где.
pitfalls: The negation comes after 什么都, right before the verb: 我什么都不吃 — never *我不什么都吃.
Choose the negator as usual: 不 for will and habits (什么都不吃 ‘won’t eat anything’), 没 for facts (什么都没买 ‘bought nothing’), and always 什么都没有 with 有.
subtleties: 什么都 is a phrase, not one word: 什么 ‘what’ + 都 ‘all’. With 不 / 没 it means ‘nothing’, without a negation ‘everything’; it is kept as one entry for the concept ‘nothing’.
Without a negation it means ‘everything’: 他什么都吃 ‘he eats everything’.
什么都 stands before the verb even though it is the object: 我什么都不要 ‘I don’t want anything’.

senses.def: nobody, no one (‘there is no one who …’)

examples.py: Méiyǒu rén zhīdào tā zài nǎr.

synonyms.nuance: méi rén: the short spoken form — 没人在家
shéi dōu bù + verb: ‘nobody (wants, likes …)’ — 谁都不想去 ‘nobody wants to go’

etymology.text: 没有 ‘there is not’ + 人 ‘person’: ‘there is no person (who …)’.

funFacts: Like Turkish kimse yok ‘there is nobody’ (yok = ‘there is not’), Chinese says ‘nobody’ with ‘there is not’ — 没有人.
pitfalls: 没有人 opens the sentence: 没有人在家 ‘nobody is at home’ — *人没有在家 would mean ‘the person is not at home’.
As an object Chinese does not use 没有人: ‘I don’t know anybody’ is 我谁都不认识 (S10) — not *我认识没有人.
subtleties: 没有人 is a phrase, not one word: 没有 ‘there is no’ + 人 ‘person’ — literally ‘there is nobody who …’; it is kept as one entry for the concept ‘nobody’.
没有人 = ‘there isn’t anyone (who …)’; for ‘nobody wants / likes’ 谁都不 + verb is just as common.

contrasts.value: all along — mostly with a negation (从来不 ‘never’); in positive sentences rarer

profile.feeling: Firm habits and principles: ‘I have never …’, ‘he never …’.

senses.def: (with 不 / 没) never, not ever
always, all along (in positive sentences, less common)

examples.tr: I have never been to China.
He has always been like this.
He has always been very conscientious.

synonyms.nuance: cóngbù: the short written form — 他从不迟到
cóngméi: ‘never (has it happened)’, usually with 过

etymology.text: 从 ‘from’ + 来 ‘to come’: ‘from the past until now, all along’; with a negation ‘never’.

funFacts: 从来 is literally ‘from-come’: ‘from back then until now’. Like English ‘ever’, it needs a negation to mean ‘never’: 从来不 = ‘not ever’.
pitfalls: 从来 alone is not ‘never’: say 我从来不吃肉 — *我从来吃肉 is wrong.
For what has never happened use 从来没 + verb + 过 (过 comes in S14): 我从来没去过中国; for habits 从来不: 我从来不喝酒.
subtleties: 从来不 = never, by habit or choice; 从来没 = it has never happened.

senses.def: nor; and not … either (不 A，也不 B = neither A nor B)

examples.py: Wǒ bù hē chá, yě bù hē kāfēi.
examples.tr: I drink neither tea nor coffee.

examples.py: Tā bù chī ròu, yě bù chī yú.
examples.tr: He eats neither meat nor fish.

examples.py: Tā jì bù chōuyān, yě bù hē jiǔ.
Nǐ bú qù? Wǒ yě bú qù.
examples.tr: You’re not going? I’m not either.

synonyms.nuance: yě méi: the same with 没 — for facts and with 有: 我没有哥哥，也没有姐姐

etymology.text: 也 ‘also’ + 不 ‘not’: ‘also not’ — neither, nor.

funFacts: German has weder … noch, Turkish ne … ne, Russian ни … ни; Chinese has no special pair — it says ‘not … also not …’: 不 … 也不 ….
pitfalls: 也 stands before 不: 我也不喝 — never *我不也喝.
With 有 and with past facts it is 也没: 我没有哥哥，也没有姐姐; 他没吃肉，也没吃鱼.
subtleties: 也不 is a phrase, not one word: 也 ‘also’ + 不 ‘not’. Repeated (不 A，也不 B) it gives ‘neither A nor B’; it is kept as one entry because the pair works as the ‘nor’ of the course.
既不 … 也不 … is more formal and emphatic than 不 … 也不 ….
Before a 4th tone it is said yě bú: 也不要, 也不是.

lexemes.role: 也不 is a phrase, not one word: 也 ‘also’ + 不 ‘not’. Repeated (不 A，也不 B) it gives ‘neither A nor B’; it is kept as one entry because the pair works as the ‘nor’ of the course.

features.toneSandhi: yě bú before a 4th-tone syllable (也不是, 也不去); yě bù before the others (也不吃)

absent.reason: Chinese has no determiner meaning ‘no, not any’ (German kein, Greek κανένας): the verb is negated and the noun stays bare.
absent.use: 没有 + noun for ‘have no / there is no’: 我没有哥哥 ‘I have no older brother’, 这里没有盐 ‘there is no salt here’ (一个 drops out); with other verbs 不 / 没 + verb + noun: 我不吃肉 ‘I eat no meat’.
